Senses.Explanation: For two parties to deceive or lead each other astray. Zen records repeatedly place this ordinary reciprocal act under negation in the assurance, ‘Only provide the assenting heart; we certainly will not deceive one another’ (但辦肯心。必不相賺), with graphic variants in the verb ‘provide’ and the adverb ‘certainly.’ Yuanwu Keqin closes an address with that formula. Dahui Zonggao uses it after answering an interlocutor's request about how to receive and keep a statement. Zhongfeng Mingben quotes the old formula and elsewhere tells a Zen student to trust his words because they will not deceive one another. Puan Yinsu repeats the assurance, but also asks whether an old worthy's saying amounts to mutual deception (古人恁麼道。莫是相賺麼). Affirmative, negative, and interrogative forms retain the same reciprocal act; the Zen-specific bend is the formula's recurring use as a public assurance tied to an assenting heart.

Senses.Explanation: to touch or meet the eye; in context, whatever meets the eye. It forms public questions—'what is the affair that meets the eye?' and 'what is awakening that meets the eye?'—to which Xuefeng answers with a question, 'what is it?', with 'heavens!', by lifting the whisk, or by pointing out a bare pillar. Yunmen's statement 'even if whatever meets the eye is unobstructed' becomes a repeatedly quoted and tested formula. One later master raises a whisk and says that calling it a whisk leaves obstruction in what meets the eye, while not calling it a whisk does too. Linji's record says 'whatever meets the eye is it,' and immediately supplies its own stated obstruction: feelings arise, knowledge separates, and thought changes the object. The ordinary visual phrase is thus heavily loaded as interview and teaching-seat vocabulary.

Senses.Explanation: Masters raise ‘awakening wherever the eye lands’ as a public question, then enact or redirect the answer through an immediately visible object or action without making one response universal. The graphs say “meet or strike the eye” and “awakening”: “awakening wherever the eye meets.” The exact question “What is awakening wherever the eye meets?” accounts for 69 of the headword’s 127 occurrences. The answers and follow-up actions vary. When Shishuang Qingzhu asks Daowu, Daowu calls a novice, tells him to add water to the clean-water jar, later asks Shishuang what he had just asked, and leaves as Shishuang begins to repeat it; the narrative then says Shishuang woke up. Another exchange answers, “All things constantly abide”; when asked what that means, the named record subject answers with the headword again. Elsewhere the answer is “the buddha hall before you,” a named record subject kicks a dog so that it runs off making a sound, or Xuansha says, “Before a dead monk is precisely awakening wherever the eye meets.” Linquan’s later comment on the Daowu case says that it has “no empty gap.” The records preserve these named exchanges and different predicates; this entry gives no single explanation in place of their different answers.

Senses.Explanation: To become obstructed along every route or at every turn. The phrase diagnoses fixation, conceptual impurity, mishandled teaching formulas, or ongoing course that converts whatever it meets into an impediment. Huanglong says an object lodged in the chest remains before the eyes and produces obstruction at every turn. Dahui says mixed poison entering the mind makes one obstructed wherever one turns. Linquan warns that inadequate grounding in Caodong teaching repeatedly meets obstruction. Yunju contrasts realization’s unimpeded function with loss, which produces obstruction everywhere.

Senses.Explanation: (諸佛出身處) is “the place from which the buddhas emerge,” a stock question in recorded encounters. The question is normally spoken by an unnamed monk, while different masters answer locally: “East Mountain walks on the water,” “a donkey womb and horse belly,” “you asked very fittingly,” and other incompatible replies. The corpus therefore fixes the interrogative formula but supplies no single shared place-name as its answer. Later raisers explicitly quote Yunmen’s question-and-answer as an inherited case.

Senses.Explanation: Having no route by which devas can offer flowers marks conduct with no exposed place for heavenly praise to fasten onto; the paired outsiders likewise find no opening to spy. Yuanwu Keqin uses the pair for one whose discriminating machinery is extinguished and whose conduct has become ordinary. Dahui Zonggao contrasts meticulous rule-keeping that earns heavenly food with the ancestral gate, where devas have no route to bring flowers. Chushi Fanqi uses it for unhindered conduct that neither clings to brightness nor liberation.

Senses.Explanation: Dayu Shouzhi answers “what is buddha?” with “saw apart a steelyard weight.” Later masters preserve the physically resistant image while warning that turning the phrase into a ready-made idea is itself conceptual thought; the resistance does not make the weight merely unreal. Four works preserve the headword in complete local sentences rather than as an unanchored quotation. The saying turns a dense everyday object into an answer-demanding impossibility: ordinary tools cannot open what has no seam. The gloss stays at the level supported by those uses; it does not import a fixed religious resolution from outside the corpus.

Senses.Explanation: When an unnamed monk asks what buddha is, Cuiyan Shouzhi—identified in the source at Dayu Mountain—answers, 'saw open a scale weight.' Dahui Zonggao later lists Cuiyan Shouzhi's reply among compact answer-lines that point a listener toward the road, and raises it in two further addresses. Huaiyu Yongxuan separately opens a verse on Cuiyan's answer with the same line; two lamp records preserve that one verse. The sources establish a concrete saw-and-weight answer and its later quotation, not a general claim that scale weights are impossible to cut.
